title: Simplicity
tomorrow: give to everyone who asks, or know who you're giving to?

segments.voice: Yesterday, debt: a king who forgave ten thousand talents, and a servant who couldn't forgive a hundred pence. The line was forgive us our debts. Today, a man with the opposite problem: too much.

A closet door that needs a shoulder to close. A storage unit for whatever didn't fit. A phone warning that storage is almost full. Luke tells of a farmer with the same problem, after a harvest so big he has nowhere to put it. And there's something odd in the way the story is told. Listen for who he talks to. In the whole scene, he has one conversation partner, and it's himself. So how does a farmer with full barns end up called a fool? Not for the size of his harvest.
screen: `A CLOSET THAT WON'T CLOSE.` → `NOWHERE TO PUT IT.` → `WHO DOES HE TALK TO?`

segments.voice: Luke says he thought within himself. Then the plan, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "I will pull down my barns, and will build greater." Then he speaks to his own soul: "Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years: take thy rest; eat, drink, make good cheer." No family, no workers, no neighbor in the conversation. Every line runs from I to my. Then the only other voice in the story arrives: "Thou fool, this night do they require thy soul of thee." That's the puzzle solved. He isn't a fool for farming well. Jesus gives the point before the story even starts: "a man's life doth not consist in the abundance of things which he possesseth." The harvest didn't make him wicked. It made him alone. Bigger barns, and no room left for anybody else. Saint Basil the Great, preaching on this parable, said the bread kept back in storage belongs to the hungry, and the coat hanging unused belongs to someone who has none. The Catechism names the inner side of it poverty of heart: letting go of attachment to things, so there's room for God and for other people. Simplicity here isn't owning nothing. It's keeping space in your life for someone besides yourself. The barn can be a closet, a storage unit, or a phone full of things never opened again.
screen: `HE TALKS ONLY TO HIMSELF.` · `I WILL PULL DOWN MY BARNS.` · `THOU FOOL, THIS NIGHT.` · `THE UNUSED COAT BELONGS TO SOMEONE.` · then, large: `MORE ROOM.`

segments.voice: Look around the room you're in and let your eyes land on three things you haven't used in a long while. Rest your gaze on each one for a breath and ask who could use it. If you pray, you can offer the three to God before you let them go.
Simplicity. Having less than has you: room cleared for God and for other people, the opposite of the bigger barn.
Your line: more room. The farmer built bigger barns and kept space for nobody. Till tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics speak of poverty of heart, freedom from attachment to things; some keep it by giving away what they don't use, especially in Lent, through parish clothing drives and Catholic charities.

chat.meaning: The farmer's barns grew while his life shrank to himself. Simplicity clears room for God and for others; it isn't owning nothing.
